content: 1. Mobile clinics and innovative models of eye care should be strengthened to provide services in geographically challenging areas. For example, combining eye and ear care in a single mobile clinic or selected fixed facilities can enhance accessibility. 2. Member States can adopt a tailored menu of eye care services to be delivered at various levels of health facilities, depending on the local context. Awareness creation, health promotion, and education should be emphasized at all levels of care, particularly at the primary level. 3. The package of eye care interventions provides a comprehensive set of evidence-based eye care strategies across the continuum of care, along with the necessary material resources for implementation. 4. Surgical management of diabetic retinopathy (DR) and glaucoma, corneal transplants, advanced low-vision care, contact lenses, and management of complex eye conditions such as keratoconus and refractive surgeries are critical components of tertiary-level care. 5. Eye care services should be integrated into school and college systems, with collaboration among physicians, diabetologists, ministries of labor, NGOs, and primary health care providers to ensure comprehensive care for individuals aged 40–59 years. This includes health promotion for diabetes prevention, provision of spectacles for uncorrected refractive errors and presbyopia, comprehensive glaucoma examinations, laser treatments for DR and glaucoma, and cataract surgeries. 6. For individuals aged 60 and above, services should include cataract detection, management of comorbidities, provision of spectacles post-cataract surgery, and health education to promote healthy aging. Comprehensive glaucoma examinations, laser treatments for DR and glaucoma, advanced low-vision care, and integration with other specialists (e.g., hearing, injuries, mental health) are also essential. 7. Eye care interventions at different levels of care should address specific conditions. For example, primary care should focus on awareness creation and screening, while secondary and tertiary care should include clinical diagnosis, surgeries, and advanced management techniques. 8. Childhood blindness prevention requires screening of high-risk groups, health promotion to prevent vitamin A deficiency, and education to promote immunization and neonatal care. Screening for retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma, and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) using tele-ophthalmology is critical, along with follow-up care and surgical management of pediatric eye conditions. 9. Diabetic retinopathy care involves screening high-risk groups, monitoring for hypertension, and using tele-ophthalmology for DR detection. Laser treatments, injections, and follow-up care are essential, along with retinal surgeries and tele-ophthalmology models for ongoing care. 10. Glaucoma management includes screening high-risk groups, comprehensive eye examinations for diagnosis, medical and surgical treatments, and management of complex cases. 11. Corneal care involves screening and referral, health promotion to prevent eye injuries, education on eye donation, first aid for chemical injuries, medical management of corneal infections, and advanced procedures such as corneal transplants and eye banking. 12. Trachoma prevention includes screening high-risk groups, promoting facial cleanliness and sanitation, antibiotic distribution, and trichiasis surgery. 13. Low vision and rehabilitation services should include case detection, counseling, community-based rehabilitation, promotion of assistive devices and technology, and provision of low-vision care and devices. 14. Eye care services must be coordinated and integrated with other health services to meet the needs and preferences of individuals at all levels of care. This includes collaboration across sectors, such as maternal and child health, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and disability services. 15. Strengthening the eye health workforce is critical. This includes mapping workforce gaps, developing competency-based frameworks, establishing multidisciplinary teams, and ensuring task delegation and technology use for cross-functional care delivery. 16. Policies should be developed to ensure access to affordable and quality eye care services, minimize out-of-pocket expenses, and integrate eye health data into national health information systems. 17. Investment in research, innovation, and capacity building in eye health is essential to achieve sustainable development goals and improve access to universal comprehensive eye care. 18. Monitoring and evaluation frameworks should be established to assess progress toward eye care objectives, with indicators, baselines, and targets integrated into national health plans. 19. WHO provides technical resources, such as the Eye Care Situation Analysis Tool (ECSAT), to support Member States in implementing integrated people-centered eye care (IPEC) strategies.
